rewritten_text:
Tom enrolled in the newly formed Cadets of Temperance, drawn by the splendid appearance of their “regalia.” He pledged to give up smoking, chewing, and swearing for the duration of his membership. He now learned something new: the surest way to make a person yearn to do a thing is to have him promise not to do it. Before long Tom was plagued by a longing to drink and curse. It became so fierce that only the prospect of parading in his red sash prevented him from resigning. The Fourth of July was approaching; but he soon abandoned that hope—before he had borne his fetters for forty-eight hours—and placed his expectations on old Judge Frazer, the justice of the peace. The Judge appeared to be dying, and his lofty office would ensure a grand public funeral. For three days Tom showed profound interest in the Judge’s health and thirsted for reports. At times his hopes soared so high that he dared take out his regalia and rehearse before the mirror. But the Judge’s condition had a most disheartening habit of varying. Finally he was declared to be improving, and then recovering. Tom felt disgusted and distinctly wronged. He tendered his resignation immediately; that very night the Judge relapsed and died. Tom determined never again to put faith in such a man.

The funeral was a splendid affair. The Cadets marched in a fashion that might have killed their former member with envy. Still, Tom was once more a free boy, and that counted for something. He might drink and swear now, yet discovered with surprise that he had no wish to do either. Mere permission had robbed them of both their attraction and their charm.

Tom soon noticed, to his astonishment, that the vacation he had so coveted was beginning to weigh upon his hands.

He undertook a diary; but three days passed without an event, and he gave it up.

The earliest negro minstrel show arrived in town and created a stir. Tom and Joe Harper assembled their own company of performers, which kept them happy for two days.

Even the Glorious Fourth proved something of a disappointment. Heavy rain prevented the procession, and Mr. Benton, a real United States Senator and, in Tom’s estimation, the greatest man alive, fell disastrously short of expectation: he was not twenty-five feet tall, nor anything approaching it.

Then a circus arrived.

“Besides, few people except sailors can tie this knot, and it is a particular feature of Maltese sailors. I found the ribbon at the bottom of the lightning rod. It could not have belonged to either of the dead women. Suppose I am mistaken in concluding from it that the Frenchman was a sailor on a Maltese ship. Even then, the words I used in the advertisement can do no harm. He will simply assume that some detail has misled me and will not bother to investigate. If I am right, however, I have gained a considerable advantage. The Frenchman knows about the murder, though he is innocent of it, so he will naturally hesitate to answer the advertisement and claim the orangutan. His thoughts will run like this: ‘I am innocent, and I am poor. My orangutan is extremely valuable—a fortune to a man in my position. Why should I lose it over an unfounded fear of danger? Here is my chance to recover it. It was found in the Bois de Boulogne, far from the scene of the slaughter. Who could suspect an animal of doing such a thing? The police are baffled; they have not found a single clue. Even if they trace the animal, they cannot prove I knew of the murder or make me guilty because I knew. Above all, someone knows who I am. The advertiser identifies me as the animal’s owner, and I cannot be sure how much more he knows. If I fail to claim such valuable property when someone knows it belongs to me, I will make the animal, at least, look suspicious. Drawing attention to either of us would be unwise. I will answer the advertisement, collect the orangutan, and keep it hidden until the trouble has passed.’”

Just then we heard footsteps on the stairs.

“Keep your pistols ready,” Dupin said, “but do not draw or fire them unless I give the signal.”

The house’s front door had been left open. Our visitor had come in without ringing and climbed a few steps. Now he appeared to hesitate. Soon we heard him going down again. Dupin was hurrying toward the door when the footsteps began climbing once more. This time the visitor did not turn back. He came up firmly and knocked on the door of our room.

“Come in,” Dupin called, warmly and cheerfully.

A man entered, plainly a sailor. He was tall, broad, and muscular, with a reckless expression that was not altogether unattractive.

“Now, then, tell me everything.”

“Well, you see, this is how it happened. My old mistress—that’s Miss Watson—she’s always picking on me and treats me pretty harshly. But she always said she wouldn’t sell me down to New Orleans. Lately, though, I’d noticed a slave trader coming around quite a lot, and I began to worry. Then one night I crept up to the door, pretty late, and it wasn’t quite shut. I heard my mistress telling the widow she was going to sell me down to New Orleans. She said she didn’t want to, but she could get eight hundred dollars for me, and it was too much money to resist. The widow tried to make her promise not to do it, but I didn’t wait to hear any more. I got away in a hurry, I can tell you.

“I ran down the hill, expecting to steal a small boat somewhere along the bank above town. But people were still moving about, so I hid in the old, falling-down barrel maker’s shop beside the river, waiting for everyone to leave. Well, I stayed there all night. There was always somebody around. Boats began passing at about six in the morning, and by eight or nine everybody in them was talking about your father coming into town and saying you’d been killed. Those later boats were full of ladies and gentlemen crossing over to look at the place. Sometimes they stopped at the bank to rest before going across, and I learned everything about the killing from their talk. I was terribly sorry you were dead, Huck, but I’m not sorry anymore.

“I lay under the wood shavings all day. I was hungry, but I wasn’t scared. I knew my mistress and the widow were leaving for the camp meeting right after breakfast and would be away all day. They know I go out with the cattle around daybreak, so they wouldn’t expect to see me at the house. They wouldn’t miss me until after dark. The other servants wouldn’t miss me either, because they’d slip away and take a holiday as soon as the old folks were gone.

“Well, after dark I went along the river road for two miles or more, until there weren’t any houses. I’d decided what to do. You see, if I kept trying to escape on foot, the dogs could follow my trail. If I stole a boat to cross the river, they’d notice it was missing. Then they’d know roughly where I’d come ashore on the other side and where to start tracking me.”
